title: How a Ditch in the Desert Became the World's Most Important Shortcut

youtube.title: How a Ditch in the Desert Became the World's Most Important Shortcut
youtube.description:
In March 2021 a single ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days and held up billions of dollars of trade every day. This is the story of how a canal dug through the Egyptian desert became one of the most important places on Earth.

(Test episode from the automated pipeline.)

paragraphs.text: In March 2021, one of the largest container ships in the world turned sideways in a narrow channel in Egypt.
The Ever Given was about 400 meters long. For six days, it blocked the Suez Canal, and hundreds of ships waited at both ends.
Suddenly, the whole world was watching a narrow strip of water.
By one estimate, around 9.6 billion dollars of goods were held up every single day.
So how did a ditch in the desert become one of the most important places on Earth?
For most of history, ships sailing between Europe and Asia had to go all the way around Africa.
Then, in 1869, a French-led company opened a canal straight through Egypt, linking Port Said on the Mediterranean to the city of Suez on the Red Sea.

shots.prompt: 19th century oil painting of steamships entering a newly opened canal in the desert, flags and crowds on the banks

paragraphs.text: The project was driven by the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, and it took about ten years of digging.

shots.prompt: 19th century oil painting of thousands of workers digging a canal through the desert, steam dredgers, dust, wide view

paragraphs.text: Overnight, the sea route between Europe and Asia became thousands of kilometers shorter.
When it opened, the canal was about 164 kilometers long. After later expansions, it now measures around 193 kilometers.
In 1888, the major powers signed an agreement that promised free passage to every ship, in war and in peace.

shots.quote: The Suez Maritime Canal shall always be free and open, in time of war as in time of peace, to every vessel of commerce or of war, without distinction of flag.
shots.author: Convention of Constantinople, 1888

paragraphs.text: But in 1956, Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, nationalized the canal company, partly to pay for a huge new dam on the Nile.
Britain, France and Israel invaded. Pressure from the United States and the Soviet Union soon forced them to withdraw.
Then, after the Six-Day War in 1967, the canal closed for eight years. More than a dozen ships were trapped inside the whole time.

shots.prompt: oil painting of a group of old cargo ships anchored together in a wide desert lake, dusty and abandoned, 1970s

paragraphs.text: In normal times, roughly 12 percent of global trade passes through the Suez Canal, from oil and gas to cars, clothes and electronics.
When it closes, ships are forced onto the long route around Africa, which can add more than a week to a journey.
For Egypt, the tolls are one of the country's most important sources of foreign currency.
A canal dug more than 150 years ago still decides how quickly the world gets its goods.
This is the story of the Suez Canal.
